**What went wrong and how it was fixed:**

1. `cp -al releases/current candidates/next` created a genuine **hardlink** (link count went 1→2 on the release file; the differing inode numbers were an overlayfs reporting artifact).
2. `artifactctl stamp` opens the file `r+b` and writes in place — it does not replace the file. So stamping the candidate **also rewrote the release's header to NEXT**, despite the paths differing. The claim "paths differ so only the copy will change" only holds when the copy has its own inode; hardlinks share one.

Takeaway: `cp -al` saves copy cost only for files you will never modify in place. Since `stamp --in-place` mutates bytes, the firmware must be de-linked (real copy) before stamping — which is now the case, so future stamps of the candidate cannot touch the release.
